# How to Make an AI Short Film in Picsart, from Idea to Final Cut

> **In short:** Picsart's AI short film maker turns your idea into a finished film of 15 seconds to 10 minutes. According to Picsart, you approve each stage along the way, and you download the final cut as an MP4 video file.

Have you ever wanted to see a story you made up actually play on screen, but felt you needed a camera crew, an animator, and a free weekend? An AI short film maker tries to handle the heavy lifting, while you stay in charge of the story. Picsart's tool is built around that idea, and it's more approachable than it sounds.

This guide walks you through the whole process, one stage at a time.

## Before you start

You'll need a Picsart account and access to the AI short film maker, which lives inside Picsart. The announcement doesn't spell out which plans or app versions include it, so check the app before you invest time in a story.

Have these three things ready:

- **A premise.** That's your core idea, written in two or three sentences: who the hero is, what goes wrong, and the tone of the ending.
- **A visual style.** The tool offers eight styles to choose from.
- **A running time.** You can pick anything from 15 seconds up to 10 minutes. Start short.

## What makes a short film idea work

Short films reward restraint. Every extra character, location, or side plot is one more thing the AI has to keep consistent from scene to scene, so keep your first idea small.

- **One idea you can say in a breath.** If you can't summarize it in a sentence, it's probably too big.
- **A clear setup, escalation, and payoff.** Something goes wrong, someone reacts, and the ending lands.
- **Two or three characters.** That's enough for conflict without crowding the frame.
- **One or two locations.** A tight setting helps the world stay steady.
- **A tone word.** Words like "comedy" or "warm payoff" tell the story writer what ending to build toward.

💬 Example premise: *"A nervous baker has one hour to save a wedding cake that collapsed. Her grumpy father helps her fix it. The tone is warm, with a funny payoff."*

## Step 1 — Write your idea and set up the film

Find the "Start with an Idea" box in the AI short film maker. Type your two or three sentences there. Then add a title and pick one of the eight styles.

Next, set the length from 15 seconds to 10 minutes, and choose either 9:16 (vertical, for phone feeds) or 16:9 (wide, for YouTube-style viewing). Pick a dialogue language too.

The announcement also says you choose a writing model, an image model, and a video model in the film settings before you start. The writing model drafts the story and dialogue, the image model draws characters and locations, and the video model animates the scenes. Set all three before you continue.

For your first film, keep "Review each step" turned on. That gives you a checkpoint at every stage. Then press Create story.

💬 Tip for the title field: *"The Wedding Cake Rescue"* is short, clear, and easy to remember.

**You'll know it worked when** the tool starts building your story and you see the next stage appear.

## Step 2 — Review and refine the story

The story writer returns a synopsis and a scene list. The scene list includes story beats (the key moments of the plot) and scene directions (notes on what happens in each shot).

Read through it and check two things. First, does your setup and payoff still come through? Second, is the cast still small? If the writer added extra characters, ask it to trim them.

You can edit the text directly, or type a change into the "Refine your story" box. For example: *"Keep it to the baker and her father, and end with the cake being served."* When it reads the way you want, approve the story.

**You'll know it worked when** the synopsis matches your premise and the scene list follows one clear storyline.

## Step 3 — Approve the cast and location

Next, the tool creates a reference sheet for each character. A reference sheet shows full-body views and close-ups of the face, so the AI has a fixed look to follow for every scene. You'll also get a reference for the location.

Check each face, outfit, and prop. If something looks off, click the pencil icon to adjust it, or try a different cast model. Once you're happy, approve the cast.

Pay special attention to details you'll need later, like a hat, a necklace, or a specific cake. These references are what keep those details steady across the whole film.

💬 Example adjustment: *"Give the father a gray cardigan and reading glasses. The baker wears a white apron with a flour stain."*

**You'll know it worked when** each character looks like the same person in every view, and the location matches your setting.

## Step 4 — Check storyboard continuity

Each episode gets six storyboard frames, which are still drawings that preview the shots. Before anything moves, the tool runs a continuity check. Continuity means the details stay the same from one shot to the next.

The check flags problems such as missing clothing or a prop in the wrong hand. You have three options: make a targeted repair, redraw the set, or animate anyway. Fixing a problem at the storyboard stage is much easier than fixing it after the video is made.

💬 Example fix: *"The cake should be on the table, not in the father's hands, in frame three."*

**You'll know it worked when** the continuity check shows no flags you care about, or you've made a conscious choice about the ones it still shows.

## Step 5 — Animate the clips

Once you approve the storyboards, they become video clips. If a clip isn't right, you don't have to start over. Ask for the change in plain language, such as "slow the camera move," and only the selected clip gets remade.

Keep your requests simple and specific. One change at a time works better than a long list, because each change is a fresh try and can shift other details.

💬 Example request: *"Slow the camera move in this clip, and keep the cake in the center of the frame."*

**You'll know it worked when** the selected clip shows your change and the other clips stay the same.

## Step 6 — Review and download the final film

The tool assembles the clips into one film. An independent review then scores the result, checking characters, outfits, props, and dialogue. It leaves timestamped notes, so you can see exactly where a problem appears.

You can keep the cut as it is, redo a single scene, or make more edits. When you're satisfied, press "Download MP4."

💬 Tip: Watch the film once on your phone, with the sound on. Problems in dialogue and timing show up more clearly that way.

**You'll know it worked when** the MP4 file saves to your device and plays from start to finish.

## Common mistakes

- **Mistake: Writing a sprawling premise with many characters.** Fix: Cut the cast to two or three, and keep one or two locations.
- **Mistake: Skipping the reference sheets.** Fix: Look closely at faces, outfits, and props before you approve, because every later scene depends on them.
- **Mistake: Asking for many changes at once.** Fix: Change one thing at a time, and use the single-clip redo so you don't remake the whole film.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: Turn a family story, a birthday sketch, or a bedtime tale into a short film you can share with people you love.
- **For your business or work**: Small creators and shop owners can build short vertical stories for social feeds, with the same character across every film.
- **If you're just getting started**: Begin with a 15-second film and keep "Review each step" on. You'll learn the process without a big commitment of time.
- **If you already use it**: Build a series. Number your episodes by season, keep the same cast, and let each new film pick up where the last one ended.

Picsart also offers a separate tool, Ren, which turns a story idea, a photo, or a clip of your own into anime. It's a different style, but it shares the same goal of helping you make video without drawing or animating by hand.

## Wrap-up

Making an AI short film in Picsart comes down to six stages: write the idea, refine the story, approve the cast, check the storyboards, animate the clips, and download the final cut. Each stage gives you a review point, so you stay in charge of what the film says.

Your next step is small. Write a two-sentence idea for a 15-second story today, and run it through Step 1. You'll see the whole process in one sitting, and you'll know what to change next time.
